# Upweight Units Who Represent Rarer Histories

Inverse-probability weighting (IPW) gives more influence to an observed unit
when its treatment, observation, or selection history was less probable given
measured covariates. The weighted sample can represent a population in which
that mechanism no longer depends on those covariates.

For binary treatment $A$, baseline covariates $L$, and propensity score
$e(L)=P(A=1\mid L)$, the unstabilized average-treatment-effect weight is

$$
\boxed{
W_i^{\mathrm{ATE}}
=\frac{A_i}{e(L_i)}+\frac{1-A_i}{1-e(L_i)}.
}
$$

A treated unit with $e(L)=0.2$ represents five similar units; an untreated unit
with $e(L)=0.8$ also represents five. This creates a pseudo-population in which
measured $L$ is balanced across treatment, provided the score and identifying
assumptions are adequate.

IPW is an estimation strategy, not an assumption. It cannot recover
counterfactual outcomes when confounders are unmeasured, treatment versions are
ill-defined, or some target-population covariate profiles have no chance of
receiving one treatment.

# The Estimand Determines the Weights

Let $Y^a$ be the potential outcome under treatment $a$. For the average
treatment effect

$$
\operatorname{ATE}=E(Y^1-Y^0),
$$

the treatment-specific Horvitz--Thompson means are

$$
\widehat\mu_1=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{A_iY_i}{\hat e(L_i)},
\qquad
\widehat\mu_0=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(1-A_i)Y_i}{1-\hat e(L_i)},
$$

and $\widehat{\operatorname{ATE}}=\widehat\mu_1-\widehat\mu_0$.
Hájek normalization divides each weighted outcome total by its corresponding
sum of weights. It is a ratio estimator that often behaves more stably in
finite samples, though it has a different finite-sample bias structure.

For the average treatment effect among treated units,

$$
\operatorname{ATT}=E(Y^1-Y^0\mid A=1),
$$

common weights are

$$
W_i^{\mathrm{ATT}}
=A_i+(1-A_i)\frac{e(L_i)}{1-e(L_i)}.
$$

Treated units retain weight one; untreated units are weighted to resemble the
treated covariate distribution. Other choices target untreated, overlap, or
externally standardized populations. Weight formulas are therefore inseparable
from the target population.

# Why the Weighted Mean Identifies an Intervention Mean

Assume consistency, conditional exchangeability $Y^a\perp A\mid L$, positivity,
and adequate measurement. For $a=1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E\left\{\frac{AY}{e(L)}\right\}
&=E_L\left[
E\left\{\left.\frac{AY}{e(L)}\right|L\right\}
\right]\\
&=E_L\left[
\frac{P(A=1\mid L)E(Y\mid A=1,L)}{e(L)}
\right]\\
&=E_L\{E(Y^1\mid L)\}\\
&=E(Y^1).
\end{aligned}
$$

The parallel result holds for $a=0$. IPW and outcome standardization use
different nuisance models to identify the same intervention mean under their
respective assumptions. This derivation also shows the danger of a small
$e(L)$: the estimator divides by a probability near zero.

# Treatment, Censoring, Missingness, and Selection

The same principle applies to several mechanisms, but each requires its own
target and assumptions.

| Weight | Denominator models | Intended pseudo-population |
|---|---|---|
| Treatment weight | observed treatment given baseline covariates | treatment independent of measured baseline confounders |
| Censoring weight | remaining observed given prior history | follow-up independent of measured predictors of censoring and outcome |
| Missingness weight | outcome observed given measured information | observed outcomes represent eligible units |
| Selection or transport weight | study inclusion given effect-relevant covariates | study units represent a specified target population |
| Longitudinal treatment weight | each treatment given previous treatment and covariate history | observed treatment histories emulate target regimes |

For dropout indicator $R=1$, an inverse-probability-of-censoring weight may be
$1/P(R=1\mid A,L)$ among observed outcomes. Treatment and censoring weights can
be multiplied when both mechanisms must be adjusted, but the resulting
assumptions multiply too. Predictors of each mechanism and outcome must be
measured at the correct time.

# Stabilization and Longitudinal Histories

Unstabilized longitudinal weights can become highly variable because they are
products of reciprocal probabilities. For visits $t=0,\ldots,T$, a stabilized
treatment weight has the form

$$
SW_i=
\prod_{t=0}^{T}
\frac{P(A_{it}=a_{it}\mid \bar A_{i,t-1})}
{P(A_{it}=a_{it}\mid \bar A_{i,t-1},\bar L_{it})},
$$

where bars denote histories through time. The numerator preserves selected
marginal features of treatment history while the denominator adjusts for
measured time-varying confounding.

This is central when a time-varying covariate both predicts later treatment and
is affected by earlier treatment. Ordinary regression adjustment for that
covariate may block part of the earlier treatment effect while failing to
handle confounding of later treatment. A marginal structural model fitted in
the weighted pseudo-population can target effects of treatment regimes under
sequential exchangeability, sequential positivity, and correct weight models.

Stabilization can reduce variance; it does not solve structural nonpositivity or
unmeasured confounding. Truncating or winsorizing extreme weights trades some
variance reduction for bias and changes the estimator. Always report the rule
and show sensitivity to defensible thresholds.

# Building and Checking an IPW Analysis

## Define the target and independent unit

Specify the intervention, outcome time, effect scale, target population, and
whether the target is ATE, ATT, or another contrast. Identify the unit at which
treatment or selection occurs. Technical observations nested within one donor
do not receive independent causal histories.

## Estimate each probability without outcome-driven searching

Use temporally eligible variables and a causally sufficient adjustment set.
Logistic models are common, but nonlinearities and interactions may be needed.
Flexible prediction can help if it yields balance and stable estimates; a high
cross-validated classification score alone is not success.

## Diagnose the weighted pseudo-population

At minimum, inspect:

- weighted standardized differences and distributions of every important
  baseline covariate;
- propensity-score overlap within treatment groups;
- minimum, maximum, quantiles, mean, and coefficient of variation of weights;
- which units dominate weighted totals;
- the effective sample size

$$
n_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{(\sum_i w_i)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2};
$$

- whether estimated stabilized weights have a mean near the value implied by
  their construction;
- sensitivity to model form and prespecified truncation or restriction.

Balance is evaluated after weighting. Extreme weights are symptoms of sparse
support, score-model misspecification, or both. A large original sample can
have a small effective sample size after weighting.

## Fit the marginal outcome contrast with suitable uncertainty

A weighted mean or marginal regression estimates the target contrast. The
outcome model should not be interpreted as an ordinary conditional regression
in the original population. Standard errors need to account for weights,
clustering, repeated measures, and estimated nuisance functions. Robust
sandwich variance is common, but can perform poorly with few independent
clusters or highly variable weights. Design-based bootstrap procedures should
resample independent units and repeat every estimated-weight step.

# Augmentation and Double Robustness

An augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimator combines a treatment model
with outcome regressions $m_a(L)=E(Y\mid A=a,L)$. One form for $E(Y^1)$ is

$$
\widehat\mu_1^{\mathrm{AIPW}}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\hat m_1(L_i)+
\frac{A_i\{Y_i-\hat m_1(L_i)\}}{\hat e(L_i)}
\right].
$$

The estimator is consistent under standard conditions if either the propensity
model or the outcome model is correctly specified. "Doubly robust" does not
mean immune to two arbitrary biases: both models can be wrong, positivity is
still required, and unmeasured confounding remains. Flexible nuisance fitting
also requires methods such as cross-fitting and appropriate rate conditions for
valid inference.

# Bioinformatics Example: Treatment and Follow-up in a Multi-omics Cohort

Consider 240 patients in an observational cancer cohort. Treatment $A$ depends
on age, stage, performance status, center, baseline mutation burden, and renal
function. The outcome is a 12-month donor-level immune-response score from
RNA-seq and proteomics. Patients with severe progression are also more likely
to miss the 12-month biopsy.

The patient is the experimental unit. Aliquots, assay plates, sequencing lanes,
genes, proteins, and cells are technical or within-patient observations. A
defensible analysis might use:

1. treatment weights to balance measured baseline common causes of treatment
   and outcome;
2. censoring weights to represent patients whose outcomes became unobserved,
   conditional on measured history before dropout;
3. their product in a marginal donor-level outcome analysis;
4. cluster-aware uncertainty if treatment practices or sampling are correlated
   within centers.

Biological replicates are independent patients sampled from the target
population. Repeating assays improves measurement but does not improve
treatment positivity or replace missing patients. If a treatment is never used
for a disease stage at one center, extra reads cannot create the missing causal
comparison.

Statistically, the weighted effect estimates a specified population contrast
under exchangeability, positivity, consistency, and correct treatment and
censoring models. Biologically, a shift in the multi-omic score is evidence
about the prespecified molecular endpoint, not automatically tumor control,
clinical benefit, or a validated mechanism. Report absolute effect magnitude,
uncertainty, assay reliability, and replication across cohorts or perturbation
systems.

# Failure Modes and Sensitivity

| Failure | What it looks like | Appropriate response |
|---|---|---|
| Structural nonpositivity | treatment absent for a target covariate pattern | restrict or redefine target; collect comparative data |
| Practical nonpositivity | very small estimated probabilities and extreme weights | inspect support, simplify target, improve model cautiously |
| Residual imbalance | weighted covariates remain different | revise assignment model without using outcomes |
| Unmeasured confounding | good measured balance but biased effect | negative controls and quantitative sensitivity analysis |
| Informative missingness beyond measured history | censoring weights cannot recover absent outcomes | collect predictors, use sensitivity models, bound conclusions |
| Pseudoreplication | cells or genes treated as independent causal units | aggregate or model hierarchy at donor assignment level |
| Aggressive truncation | stable estimate driven by altered weights | report bias--variance trade-off and threshold sensitivity |

Compare IPW with outcome standardization and a justified augmented estimator.
Large disagreement can reveal functional-form dependence or weak support, but
agreement does not validate shared causal assumptions. Show estimates across
prespecified weight models, overlap restrictions, and truncation rules, and
distinguish a changed estimate from a changed estimand.

- [Propensity scores](propensity-scores.qmd) explains balancing scores,
  treatment-model construction, matching, and overlap diagnostics.

  determines which histories belong in each denominator model.

  clarifies the assumptions behind observation and censoring weights.
- [Standard errors](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) distinguishes
  sampling precision from bias and explains cluster-aware uncertainty.
- [Repeated measures and longitudinal data](../advanced-modeling/repeated-measures-and-longitudinal-data.qmd)
  develops dependence and dropout in longitudinal studies.

1. IPW reweights observed units by inverse assignment or observation
   probabilities to represent a specified target regime.
2. Weight formulas encode the estimand; ATE, ATT, overlap, censoring, and
   transport weights answer different questions.
3. Balance, support, weight influence, and effective sample size are essential
   diagnostics, whereas treatment prediction accuracy is secondary.
4. Stabilization and truncation can improve precision but do not repair absent
   support, unmeasured confounding, or an ill-defined intervention.
5. In omics, weights belong to independent biological units and histories, not
   to the many cells, reads, or molecular features measured within them.
